exemplar: The passage argues that Native North America was not an empty wilderness but a continent of diverse, complex societies - from the Mississippian chiefdoms to the Pueblo towns to the Iroquois Confederacy - each adapted to its environment.

The Iroquois Confederacy united five (later six) nations under the Great Law of Peace, coordinating diplomacy and warfare through a sophisticated council system that impressed even European observers.

The diversity of Native societies meant European contact produced very different outcomes: some nations became vital trading partners, others faced immediate conquest - and Native rivalries shaped every colonial war.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about Native societies before European contact.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific Native society organized itself politically or economically.
C. Briefly explain ONE way the diversity of Native societies affected European colonization.

stimulus.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
stimulus.text: Historians now stress that the Americas in 1491 were home to millions of people organized in remarkably diverse societies. In the Mississippi Valley, chiefdoms centered on mound cities like Cahokia commanded regional trade networks. In the Southwest, Pueblo peoples built sophisticated irrigation systems and multi-story towns. In the Northeast, the Iroquois Confederacy bound nations together under a constitution of peace. Along the Pacific Coast, communities thrived on salmon and cedar without ever adopting agriculture. There was no single 'Indian' way of life - only hundreds of distinct peoples, each with its own economy, politics, and beliefs, about to confront an invasion that would transform them all.

exemplar: Coolidge declares that business - commerce, industry, and profit-making - is the central concern of American life, and that government should serve and support it rather than restrain it.
The Revenue Acts of the 1920s slashed income-tax rates on the wealthy and corporations, reflecting Coolidge's belief that low taxes on business would fuel prosperity for all.
Critics argued Coolidge's philosophy ignored the era's underlying problems - farm distress, labor exploitation, and reckless speculation - leaving the economy vulnerable to the crash of 1929.
parts: A. Briefly describe Coolidge's view of the relationship between business and American life in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE policy of the 1920s that reflected Coolidge's philosophy.
C. Briefly explain ONE criticism of Coolidge's approach to business and government.

stimulus.attribution: Calvin Coolidge, address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, Washington, D.C., January 17, 1925.
stimulus.text: The chief business of the American people is business. They are profoundly concerned with producing, buying, selling, investing and prospering in the world.
